While deep learning models excel when trained extensively on data for specific events, their effectiveness often declines due to domain shifts when encountering new topics. Consequently, current detection methods face major obstacles when dealing with emergent fake news events, where accumulating large, well-annotated datasets is impractical. Furthermore, integrating knowledge about new events currently necessitates retraining models or continuous fine-tuning—a process that is often costly, inefficient, and unfeasible in real-world applications.

To solve these issues, this paper presents MetaFEND, an end-to-end framework capable of learning to identify fake news from newly emerged events using limited verified data (few-shot setting). The model combines meta-learning techniques with neural process methodologies to maximize performance. Key innovations include a proposed label embedding module for processing categorical nuances and a hard attention mechanism to filter out irrelevant content to enhance detection efficacy. Rigorous testing on multimedia datasets sourced from Twitter and Weibo demonstrates that MetaFEND effectively identifies misinformation on unseen events and surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

to explore dark matter structure formation, focusing on how velocity and density fields influence halo mass function prediction via cosmological $N$-body simulations. We trained a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on early-time data from a pure dark matter simulation to forecast particle halo masses at $z=0$ within the range $10.5 < \log(M / M_{\odot}) < 14$. For simulations adhering to standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology with an initial scalar perturbation amplitude $A_s$ and resolution matching typical values ($A_s\approx 0.5 \times$ something), velocity incorporation offered negligible improvements; specifically with original values ($A_s$ small), no substantial gain in performance against using density alone. To explore collapse mechanics including density and smaller mass impacts where velocities might vary more significantly, the research adjusted initial scaling ($A_s$ to be larger, simulating stronger initial fluctuation), enabling velocity to affect larger, yet still sub-visible scales. The results indicate notable performance improvements across velocity-enhanced scenarios with larger $A_s$. Additionally, a distinct performance gap emerged based on density kernel smoothing, suggesting velocity importance varies by density resolution. Finally, the study examined how halo formation correlates with velocities, revealing that on larger scales with larger $A_s$ and thus higher velocities, halos form later compared to low-velocity (smaller $A_s$) cases.

Within the framework of a muon collider, we reassess the validity of $W$ and $Z$ parton distribution functions (PDFs) at leading order for processes from 2 to 2n. To facilitate our analysis, we present publicly available implementations of the Effective [$W$/$Z$ and] Weizs\'acker–Williams Approximation—collectively designated the Effective Vector Boson Approximation—by integrating it into the Monte Carlo event generator \texttt{madgraph5\_amc@\nlo}. This development establishes the foundation for creating prescription strategies that combine EW matrix element matching, parton showers, and renormalized EW PDFs. Complementing further progress in this direction, we offer practical guidance for the utilization of $W$/$Z$ PDFs.
